title: Bookletising the Curriculum
author: Jon Fant
summary: Jon Fant describes his department's shift toward organising the maths curriculum into purpose-built booklets, starting with a new calculation unit called "calculating the LBHS way." The unit was designed to embed the area model for multiplication and algebraic expansion, and the use of two-coloured counters for directed number, from the very start of Year 7. What began as a modest plan to move a handful of extra students into more advanced content ended up quadrupling the number of Year 7 classes accessing the school's higher Stage 7 curriculum, from one class to four out of six. Fant credits the shift to highly planned checks for understanding and thorough prerequisite checks built into the booklet structure. He has since expanded the approach into five full units, moving his department toward the kind of Mastery Cycle described in Mark McCourt's Teaching for Mastery, with an explicit depth-over-breadth philosophy.
points: Fant's unit deliberately builds two representations in early -- vectors and two-coloured counters for directed number, and the area model for multiplication and later algebraic expansion -- so students see the same structures recur across topics.
The department actively discourages rote reliance on "BIDMAS," pushing instead for flexible understanding of the laws of arithmetic that underpin later algebraic manipulation.

The headline result is striking: what started as a plan to move one extra class into Stage 7 content ended up moving four out of six Year 7 classes there, attributed to highly planned checks for understanding and prerequisite checks built into the booklets.

Fant is candid about the cost -- the workload of producing five full units of this intentionality has been considerable -- but reports a much clearer sense of what and how students are actually being taught across the department as a result.
quotes: My initial goals were clear: to purposefully embed two key teaching approaches - the area model for multiplication and algebraic expansion and the use of two-coloured counters - from the outset.

This led to the creation of "calculating the LBHS way" – a unit designed not just to teach content, but to introduce both students and staff to our fundamental approach to calculation, and ultimately, to facilitate this broader access to Stage 7.
Crucially, we actively discourage rote reliance on "BIDMAS", instead fostering a deeper understanding of mathematical operations.
What we actually found was that if we implemented highly planned checks for understanding and thorough prerequisite checks, we could support significantly more classes.
Ultimately, we ended up with four classes out of six in Year 7 studying Stage 7, quadrupling what we had the year before.
There's no denying that the workload and pressure to produce these units have been considerable. However, seeing the payoff has been immensely rewarding.
